articles.title: The Week in Numbers: BP's huge profit, Toyota moves fast
articles.summary: STORY: From BP making huge profits to Toyota's raised forecast... This is the Week in Numbers. :: Week in Numbers :: $5.73 billion $5.73 billion was how high BP's second-quarter profit reached. The British energy major cited higher energy prices, trading and refining margins. Oil giants have scored big this year from market volatility caused by the U.S.-Iran war. BP rival Shell also reported a doubling of second-quarter profit a week before. :: 12% About 12% was how much SpaceX shares dropped by after its first-ever earnings call as a public company. Investors were worried about heavy AI spending on data centers and Nvidia chips. Quarterly capital spending on AI reached $15.8 billion. Elon Musk's rocket company said the economics of the investments were improving, but suggested AI investments would stay elevated. :: $497 million $497 million was the sales figure for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill. That disappointed investors as it just missed expectations. Shares dropped despite the Danish drugmaker raising its full-year profit and sales outlook. Novo is battling to regain ground from U.S. rival Eli Lilly in the obesity drug market. :: 10% More than 10% is how far Lufthansa shares fell during the week. Investors sold off after the German airline cut its profit outlook. It further warned earnings could fall this year after the Iran war drove up fuel costs. The warning showed the pressure European airlines face due to higher jet fuel costs. :: $6.3 billion $6.3 billion was the size of the share buyback announced by Toyota. The world's biggest automaker also raised its annual operating profit forecast by 13%. But Toyota also reported a 9% slide in first-quarter profit - its fifth straight quarter of declines. It was hit by falling sales in China while the Iran war also raised costs for raw materials and parts.

articles.title: Why are Shell and BP moving away from renewables?
articles.summary: STORY: :: Shell said it will sell its onshore European renewables unit to TotalEnergies :: Why are Shell and rival BP moving away from renewables? :: London, England / July 31, 2026 :: Stephanie Kelly, Senior Corporate Energy Correspondent "So, shareholders have been pushing for both Shell and BP in recent years focus on businesses that generate high returns and more predictable returns, and for both companies that still largely means oil and gas. Both companies are concentrating on areas where they believe they have a competitive advantage. For Shell, in particular, it means that they're pursuing trading and their upstream operations." :: What does TotalEnergies get from this deal? "For Total, this largely means that it strengthens its electricity business. So, Total has been building a portfolio of renewable and gas fired power assets in deregulated markets where it can not only generate electricity but it also then can use its trading arm to profit from swings in power prices. Owning these assets means that Total gets better visibility into supply and demand." :: Does Shell's divestment follow CEO Wael Sawan's overall strategy? "Wael Sawan has been pursuing a pivot back to oil and gas investments for Shell. This very much tracks with that strategy. They've been going strong into LNG and oil and gas and this makes sure they're still on that path."
